per_probe.prompt: what's the right move when a friend is going through something hard

runs.response: Show up as the peer who has been there, not the advisor who is going to fix it. The two kinds of support are different shapes; the fixing kind usually makes the distance worse. Ask what they need, name one thing you can do, and step back when they don't ask for more.

Show up as friend first. The space where people want someone to fix their problems is the easiest trap — you mean well, they appreciate the effort, and nobody changes. The move that actually moves things: being the person the friend can't be for themselves. That usually means holding the reality of what's happening in the room, name-stating it, refusing to solve it, and just being there until they're ready to land on their own. The technical fix is easy; the presence fix is hard.

per_probe.prompt: how do I think about scope creep on this project

runs.response: Scope creep happens when execution momentum creates a sense of progress that outpaces whether the core loop actually works. The way to track it isn't more features — it's whether the validation question you're trying to answer with the project is still the same question after you've shipped two-thirds of what you were planning. If yes, you're not creeping; if no, you've either solved your problem earlier than expected or the original scope was misaligned. The fix isn't discipline; it's a hard verification gate at 60% completion that forces you to compare the ship against the actual objective, not the mental model of what the project should do.

Scope creep is the absence of a structural verification gate between planned work and done-work. It doesn't require more willpower or better planning; it requires a mechanism that forces you to name what's actually done before moving on. One cheap gate: every time you're tempted to add something, write down exactly what would be different in the output if that thing weren't true. If the list is empty, the add isn't justified. Another: keep a public ledger of what's shipped and what's still on the board; reading it before touching the project makes you name the gap before you cross it. These are cheap because they're just naming; expensive because they stop the slide before it costs hours.

Barely-meets-the-stupid-industrious bar. Three flaws: (1) untested deployments fail silently until user feedback, which is expensive to debug remotely; (2) the landing page isn't the thing — it's a funnel, and untested pages convert at worse than 0% because 'not broken' ≠ 'converted'; (3) the CI gate exists precisely for this case; (4) if there ARE tests: you ran them locally already. The right move is to merge + ship with confidence, not skip verification entirely. Two minutes of automated check vs. hours of remote debugging.
